Conversation guide

Protection

Practice discussing barrier protection, asking questions, and stating the conditions you need to feel comfortable. You can pause if you cannot agree.

Start six-round practiceRead the guide
UnderstandPracticeGet support

Protection can be part of a clear agreement. If an important condition is not met, you can pause or stop.

Why this topic can feel awkward · Read the guide

A common concern

“What if bringing up protection interrupts the moment?”

An example of a question you might have.

Start with your needs

A conversation about protection can begin before a sexual situation. Pick a time when you both have room to think and ask questions. You might discuss what barrier protection you want, ask what your partner is comfortable with, and check whether you have what you need. Base the conversation on your needs and the activity being considered, rather than assumptions about either person's gender or anatomy. Barrier methods include condoms and dental dams; UHS information can help you explore options for the activity you are considering.

Agreement includes the conditions

If barrier protection is a condition of your consent, say so directly. You do not have to give up that boundary to keep the conversation comfortable. If you cannot agree or do not have what you need, pause or choose an activity that everyone freely wants. For questions about protection options, supplies, or your own health needs, use UHS or a trained SHEP peer educator.

Learning context: Berkeley UHS, SHEP, and PATH to Care.

About this story

A six-round story about protection, assumptions, and different preferences.

You are Jordan, spending an evening at Sam's apartment. You are both adult college students and have started talking about having sex. You want barrier protection to be part of the plan, but you are nervous about bringing it up.
